The problem with eliminating fraternities and sororities without identifying what it is about Greek life that correlates with higher levels of sexual assault is that it's unlikely to solve the problem; it will simply move it to other organizations - perhaps organizations that are even harder to monitor and reform, because they will be less known for what they are.

Instead, focus on reform and education. Broaden the range of activities that create connections and alternative living options on campuses - I know I considered joining a sorority solely to get out of the dorm; instead, I joined the Jewish Student Union, which had the same alternative living options, without the sorority life I wasn't interested in (it had its own problems, to be sure - but they were different problems).

Create a curriculum for current and potential members with an emphasis on awareness and personal responsibility. Make completion of the curriculum, with a non-Greek faculty member, a condition of rushing a fraternity or sorority, with annual refreshers, including reference to the student code of conduct and appropriate laws. Keep the issue where it's visible and treat the actual issue, instead of believing that shutting it down is the answer, that that won't cause the issue to pop up elsewhere, unknown and harder to respond to, at least in the short term.

The hardest things were my books.  I had build an entire wall of gorgeous and not so gorgeous well-loved books, many of which had crossed the country with me several times in 50 years -- "English Romantic Writers" from college with notes on Shelley, Keats and Byron in the margins.  My books on Catherine de Medici, who I had researched extensively.  Could I really get rid of them?  Should I?  Would I?  Reader, I did.  I kept enough meaningful ones for the shelves we now have - ones like the Golden Treasury of Myths and Legends that my parents gave me at age 9.  Travel books that would still be useful, along with French and Italian language books. Every beautiful art book stayed, as did books on opera and music.  Everything else went - crumbly paperback Faulkners and Edith Whartons (notes in the margins, pages almost orange from age).  I regret a few - a complete set of Dickens, some cookbooks that contained memories of great dinners past, but other than that, it is good. I've driven premium, high-end EVs since 2014. And here's what might surprise the skeptics: I've used public charging stations fewer than 10 times in all those years, and not once in the past 20 months. My daily charging routine takes all of 10 seconds: pull into my garage, plug in, and wake up with a full "tank." No gas stations. No waiting. No inconvenience.

And the economics are even more compelling

I drive approximately 1,000 miles per month. From January 2026 through today, my actual home-charging electricity cost has been $816, measured by an app connected directly to my EV and Con Edison. After subtracting $283.92 in ConEd's off-peak charging rebates, my net electricity cost is $532.08 for approximately 9,300 miles - just 5.7 cents per mile.

For a meaningful comparison, consider my wife's ICE vehicle. It requires premium gas and has an EPA-rated combined fuel economy of 27 MPG. At our current regional premium gas price of approximately $5.58 per gallon, driving the same 9,300 miles would require about 344 gallons, costing approximately $1,922, or 20.7 cents per mile.

Same distance, two very different fuel bills: $532 for my EV versus an estimated $1,922 for her ICE vehicle. That's approximately $1,390 in savings, or 72% less for electricity. 

And there's maintenance. My EV's routine maintenance has been effectively zero.  For charging backup, I have 10 Tesla Superchargers less than 5 miles away. 

After 12 years of driving an EV, I have no desire to return to an ICE vehicle.

comments.name: Sedward
comments.body: I'm not a doctor. My mother has dementia/Alzheimer's.  This set of diseases is obviously very complex.  My guess is that the brain loses the ability to effectively clear out a huge host of proteins, most obviously amyloid and tau or TDP-43, etc, but others which cause the brain to not function as effectively as before.  Just like the body of a 90 year old can no longer keep its skin smooth, and its muscles and bones strong.  If a way is found to keep the brain able to clear out its waste, I think we'll be able to prevent it, or freeze and perhaps also partially reverse it if discovered after dementia has set in.  The brain probably has thousands of proteins and hormones that help it function.  Surely the brain with Alzheimer's has protein imbalances with most if not all of them, and those imbalances will cripple the various functions of the brain to various degrees.  Fix its general ability to balance them all, and the brain will function better.  The brain may need targeted treatments to remove the bigger culprits amyloid and tau, in addition to general treatments to boost its waste removal capacity, though.

comments.body:
There are multiple solutions possible. 

1. The European solution. Restaurants, bars, etc. charge (e.g. $1) for access to their restrooms. So instead of guiltily asking for permission, people can just pay to use them. Forget idealism and what "should" be the case - if you need a restroom urgently, this is FAR better than the alternative. Bathrooms are a service to the public like any other - it should be easily available, it doesn't necessarily have to be free. 

2. We don't need every restroom to be perfect. Provide lots of cheap restrooms, even those plastic ones use on building sites. When you or you kid needs to go, they are so much better than nothing. Providing urinals for men is very simple, and that does help half the population and avoid public urination which disgusts the other half. 
These may not be super hygienic, but they meet the basic human need. You can then calmly find a place to wash your hands. Don't let perfecct be the enemy of good. 

3. Public restrooms should never be closed without an alternative. You follow signs for 10 minutes to get to one, and it just says "closed" with no suggested alternative. Operators need to understand how despicable this is - directing someone in desperate need of a restroom to follow directions and then basically saying "ha ha, we fooled you, no restroom here!" If a public restroom is closed, they need a deal with a nearby local establishment so they can say "patrons may use the restrooms at Restaurant X" or whatever.

comments.name: cds333
comments.body:
The situation with the foster child is a tragedy waiting to happen.  Such violence and sociopathy in such a young child predicts much worse things to come.  I am a criminal defense lawyer, and this child is almost certain to need one of my colleagues in ten or twelve years time.  He is very likely to be committing crimes as a juvenile.

The LW must intervene now while the child is still young enough that things have a chance of being turned around.  I recommend that she consult with a therapist who works with troubled children.  Together they can develop a plan about how best to proceed.

The LW is in a terrible, painful situation.  Of course she is right that the sister would know who reported her if she just hears from the foster agency.  Once she decides how to proceed, I think she should tell the sister what she is going to do and why.  It might be a good idea to write a letter, perhaps with the help of a therapist.  She can explain that she is acting out of love and concern and that she is available to help in any way she can.  The sister might cut her off for a while, but I think that she will eventually realize that the LW was motivated by nothing but love.  Whatever damage is done to their relationship is nothing compared to the damage that will be done eventually by this child if he is not checked.  As the child grows, he will pose a very real threat to the sister's well-being.

Something must be done.  Very, very soon.

comments.name: Suzanne
comments.body: The LW needs to start documenting every violent interaction she witnesses between the child and his foster parents. And anyone else, for that matter, because I doubt the violence is directed solely at the sister and brother-in-law. This is a toxic situation and it needs to be reported to the appropriate authorities. But "this child is a problem" won't be enough to get the attention of over-worked, under-paid government employees. Give them specific, preferably first person evidence and plenty of it.

comments.name: Christina
comments.body: The child is clearly offers behavior challenges well beyond the skillset of the foster parents, and chances are his prenatal care is to blame, but  seems like the trump card of power lies with the agency who placed the child in their care, and must monitor him and them as he matures ---to decide his future.   Sadly some children  do stay in foster care all their lives.   If  the sister and husband move forward to adopt this child, they are making that decision, as adults,  with with their eyes wide open.   Call it tough love, but I think the agency needs to be notified with a VERY CLEAR DESCRIPTION of what is happening there.  They cannot do their job without clear information on the facts of the case.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body: If the birth mother was a drug user, she was also very likely an alcohol user. Please have the child evaluated for prenatal alcohol exposure and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; hard to believe but alcohol damage is far more consequential than any polydrug use. There are strategies available to help with care, access services, etc. It is wrong and unfair to treat such a child as 'normal' when the brain has been damaged. This by no means condones the violent behavior - rather, that acceptance provides a framing in which to address the issues. The intense anger may be a manifestation of the child's frustration over having to struggle and succeed under the parents' incorrect expectations that the child is 'normal' and should not be having problems.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body:
This kind of violent behavior in a young child makes me wonder about neurological damage he may have suffered in utero from drug exposure and/or nutrient deprivation. There can be helpful therapies, supplements and medications but early intervention is best, before the behavior becomes entrenched. Giving into this kind of behavior is really giving up on the child.
We went through a similar situation with our adopted daughter, although thankfully she was not violent towards others, but rather had wild tantrums. We made sure she had a natural diet low in sugars and processed foods and high in protein and fat, a structured routine with soothing rituals and outdoor play . She calmed down in about 3 years, and has grown into an amazing adult. But in her case, her tantrums were more likely from trauma and deficiencies rather than drug exposure which I think is a lot harder to heal from.

MFA is now considered to be obsolete, the WSJ info is not very current. These comments from an AI tool on what works best today where hackers have AI tools to get past passwords are very interesting:

  1. Passkeys & FIDO2/WebAuthn: The most practical upgrade to consumer and enterprise security is the widespread adoption of passkeys. Based on public-key cryptography, passkeys bind the login attempt to the specific, verified domain (RP ID) in the browser. Because there is no shared secret (like a password) stored on a server and no code sent via SMS, an AI agent cannot guess it, brute-force it, or trick a user into handing it over.2. Hardware Security Keys: For critical infrastructure and developer accounts (like GitHub or AWS where API keys often leak), physical security keys (e.g., YubiKeys) enforcing FIDO2 offer the strongest defense against unauthorized logins.3. Zero-Trust Identity & Short-Lived Tokens: For automated systems and APIs, static credentials stored in code repositories must be eliminated entirely. Moving to short-lived, environment-bound tokens ensures that even if an AI agent discovers a credential, it becomes useless almost immediately

Bill

comments.name: Ed Williams
comments.body:
If you have your own wifi access point (the wifi transmitter, your cable router, etc) you should do at least 2 things: turn on encryption, and turn off the SSID announcement.

The first means that any user of your wifi needs the password for your wifi, they can't just connect.  Without this anyone can connect.  This is often but not always on by default, so check it.

The second means that your wifi is not spending all day every day broadcasting "I'm here and my name is..." so everybody in range can see it.  Devices can still use it, but they have to know the name of your wifi before they can connect.

If you need more security, because you have valuable stuff attached to you network, there are more complex actions you can take to control who can use it and what they do.  

If you use someone else's wifi you need to think about how much you trust them, and with what you trust them.  Probably take a few extra steps, like at minimum be sure the connect to the website uses HTTPS not just HTTP, or use a VPN.  Just realize that nothing is perfect, just better or worse.

comments.name: COHERENCE
comments.body: Breathing, slowly, deeply, and rhythmically, "coherently", is the single best form of exercise and can and should accompany all other forms of exercise, circumstances permitting. Why? because it shifts the nervous system away from sympathetic emphasis (fight and flight) and toward parasympathetic emphasis (calm, cool, and relaxed). In fact, breathing coherently facilitates relaxation of all of the low-threshold muscle motor units automatically. These are the very sensitive muscle groups that respond to the slightest nervous system potential and serve to hold us erect, keep our balance, and control the actions of the arterial tree. When we are breathing relatively rapidly and without depth, these muscle groups are chronically tense, leading to headache, stiffness, and pain. Most of us live with this omnipresent condition all the time because our breathing patterns are not conducive to relaxation.  Therefore, our muscles and our body in general is always inhibited from moving freely. In fact, because adults breathe at a rate well above 10 breaths per minute all the time, we never even get to experience what it is like not to be in this tense condition.

"Imagine a vibrant Western democracy with a deeply polarized electorate."

I can but the "vibrant democracy" part of that attribution in Germany in the twenties holds only if one has an ahistorical optimistic view. 

Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg. found assassinated in 1919; massive unemployment married to massive reparation payments demanded by the winning side (mostly French); utterly unregulated Freikorps and other paramilitary groups roaming the streets of Berlin and Munich; hyperinflation that would embarrass even the Argentinians these days, etc.

That and the hard fact that Germany had no -- absolutely none -- experience with democracy (however you define it). Nobel-prize winning author Thomas Mann even wrote a book denouncing democracy efforts in Germany (he later retracted that political stance).

If ever an effort at democracy had less chance of taking root, it was Germany in the Wiemar Republic (okay, throw in Romania, Russia, etc.). And as it continues to this day, the big money capitalists -- Krupp, Thyssen, et al -- did everything in their power to quash democracy, in no small part because they benefited from inflation.

Hardly a "vibrant democracy." A house of cards waiting to fall.
